topic: Vibe coding and directing AI tools
focus: Vocabulary, specification and context skills for directing AI tools across code, coding agents, UI, art, video, audio, voice, game design and 3D
title: The Vibe Coder's Dictionary: The Words, Specs and Prompts That Get You Exactly What You Want
department: Department of Digital Media and Art
description: A course for people who build games, apps, sites, art and sound by directing AI tools, and who want to get exactly what they picture instead of the most typical thing a model can produce. It starts with how to ask, how language models behave and which prompting habits still work in 2026, then teaches the working vocabulary of each craft (software and coding agents, interface design, image making, film and animation, audio and voice, game design, game art and 3D) and turns it into precise, testable requests, with before and after prompts and copyable prompt templates throughout. The backbone is the timeless vocabulary and standards of each field, from requirements engineering and WCAG to film grammar, loudness standards and glTF, and every claim is marked as established fact, dated vendor guidance or practitioner opinion, because tools change faster than books. You build one small game, Lamplighter, from first spec to finished project across the twelve chapters.
prerequisites: Regular use of at least one AI chat assistant (for example Claude or ChatGPT)
Willingness to install and try a coding agent or an image, video or audio generator
No programming, art or audio training is assumed
objectives: Rewrite a vague request as a six-part spec with goal, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, examples and output format, for code, interfaces, images and sound, using requirements engineering’s terms (verifiable requirement, constraint, non-functional requirement, definition of done, Given/When/Then).
Explain tokens, context windows and context rot, sampling, reasoning effort, hallucination and sycophancy, and change a prompt or a setting because of each.

Apply current prompting patterns (examples, delimiters, structured output, chaining, critique), tell established findings from dated vendor guidance and practitioner lore, and replace outdated tips such as ALL-CAPS emphasis, prefill, “think step by step” and temperature 0.
Write bug reports, feature requests and review notes a coding agent can act on, using correct software and version-control terms.
Set up a coding agent’s context with a short project instruction file, skills, subagents, hooks and MCP servers, under permissions that limit prompt-injection risk.
Specify screens, components, states, motion and accessibility targets in the terms designers and developers use.
Direct image, video, music, sound-effect and voice generators with exact craft terms and each tool’s documented controls, dated.
Describe game feel, levels and 2D and 3D assets in measurable units, and run a small project end to end with a PRD, evals, reviews and a versioned prompt log.

chapters.title: How to Ask Exactly
chapters.summary: Why vague requests fail, and the six parts of a spec (goal, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, examples, output format) that turn a wish into something an AI can build, check and revise, for code, interfaces, images and sound alike; taught in requirements engineering’s own terms (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148’s verifiable requirement, constraint, non-functional requirement, definition of done, Gherkin’s Given/When/Then) and introducing the book’s three kinds of claim.
chapters.challenge: Take three prompts you actually sent an AI this month (one for code, one for an image or a sound, one for an interface). Rewrite each with the chapter’s Prompt kit, rerun both versions, and score both results against your acceptance criteria. Then write the one-page spec for the first playable build of Lamplighter and its first scoped revision.

sections.title: Why vague prompts fail
sections.summary: Underspecification, ambiguity and defaults: what a model does with the gaps you leave, why current models take your words literally, and the evidence that people new to prompting leave many gaps.

sections.title: The anatomy of a spec
sections.summary: Goal, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, examples and output format, what each part prevents, how requirements engineers judge a requirement, and why the same six parts work for a game build, an image and a sound.

sections.title: Acceptance criteria and examples
sections.summary: Writing “done” as checks you or the agent can run, Given/When/Then scenarios, and how a few well-chosen examples teach format and edge cases.

sections.title: Output format and the first revision
sections.summary: Asking for the deliverable in a shape you can use (structured outputs rather than the retired prefill trick), assumption lists and interviews, and revisions that change only what you name.

chapters.title: How Language Models Work, for People Who Prompt Them
chapters.summary: The machinery that changes how you should write to a model: tokens and the context window, sampling, reasoning and effort, hallucination and sycophancy, taught as durable research vocabulary (tokenization, next-token prediction, temperature and nucleus sampling, chain of thought, lost in the middle) with each vendor’s settings and limits given as dated guidance.
chapters.challenge: Run one Lamplighter prompt three times unchanged, once at a lower and once at a higher effort setting, and once with a long irrelevant document pasted in front of it. Write a half-page note explaining the differences in this chapter’s terms, and a dated model-choice note for three Lamplighter tasks backed by your own small comparison.

sections.title: Tokens, context windows and context rot
sections.summary: What a token is, why limits and prices are counted in tokens, why accuracy can fall as the context fills (the peer-reviewed “lost in the middle” finding, and “context rot” as a practitioner and vendor term), and where to put documents and questions.

sections.title: Sampling and the settings that are disappearing
sections.summary: Next-token prediction, temperature and top-p (nucleus sampling, Holtzman and colleagues, 2020) as established concepts, why the same prompt gives different answers, and, as dated vendor fact, which newest Claude and Gemini models reject or ignore these settings (October 2026).

sections.title: Reasoning models, thinking and effort
sections.summary: Models that think before they answer, chain-of-thought research (Wei and colleagues; Kojima and colleagues, 2022) and what later studies found on newer models, and the effort and thinking-level controls vendors now document (dated), which is why “think step by step” is now a legacy habit for reasoning models.

sections.title: Hallucination, sycophancy and choosing a model
sections.summary: Why models state false things fluently and agree too easily (hallucination and sycophancy, with the research behind each), the grounding habits that reduce both, and how to compare models for a task with your own small eval instead of last year’s rankings.

chapters.title: Prompting Patterns That Work, and Tips That Stopped Working
chapters.summary: The patterns that current Anthropic, OpenAI and Google documentation agree on (system prompts and roles, examples and delimiters, structured output with JSON Schema, chaining and critique), each labeled as vendor guidance, research finding or practitioner habit, and a myth-busting tour of advice that has gone out of date, with what the evidence actually shows.
chapters.challenge: Build a small Lamplighter prompt library: one prompt per pattern in this chapter, each with a before version, an after version and one sentence on what changed. Then audit an old prompt of yours for the outdated tips in Section 3.4, rewrite it, and compare the two on the same three test inputs.

sections.title: System prompts, roles and the reason behind instructions
sections.summary: Message roles and the chain of command as vendors document them, when a role sets useful tone and focus, the peer-reviewed evidence (Zheng and colleagues, 2024) that personas do not reliably raise factual accuracy, and why a reason does more work than an order.

sections.title: Examples, references and delimiters
sections.summary: Few-shot, one-shot and zero-shot prompting, the research showing that example order and format sway results, reference files and images, XML tags and headings as delimiters, and putting long material first and the question last (vendor guidance, dated).

sections.title: Structured output, chaining and critique
sections.summary: Structured outputs and JSON Schema (an open standard, 2020-12) for machine-readable results, prompt chaining into checked steps, rubric-based self-review, and asking for critique in ways that resist sycophancy.

sections.title: Myths and outdated tips
sections.summary: ALL-CAPS and “CRITICAL: MUST”, threats and tips, “think step by step”, prefill, temperature 0, “be thorough”, lists of don’ts and endless corrections in one chat: for each, where the tip came from, what current evidence and dated vendor guidance say, and whether it is a myth, model-specific or still useful.

chapters.title: Software and Code Vocabulary
chapters.summary: The standard words developers use for the parts of a program and the way work on it is organized (client and server, HTTP methods and status codes, JSON, state, modules, dependencies, Semantic Versioning 2.0.0, and Git’s own terms from repository to pull request), defined from reference documentation such as MDN Web Docs and Pro Git, so you can direct a coding agent and understand its answers.
chapters.challenge: Write a bug report and a feature request for Lamplighter in the formats from this chapter, have a coding agent act on them on a new branch with a failing test first, and review its pull request using the chapter’s checklist.

sections.title: Frontend, backend, APIs and data
sections.summary: Client and server, HTTP requests, methods and status codes, endpoints and APIs, databases and files, and the data formats (JSON, CSV) that move between them, with MDN Web Docs definitions.

sections.title: State, components and structure
sections.summary: State and events, components and modules, dependencies and package manifests, Semantic Versioning (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH), configuration and the build.

sections.title: Bugs, refactors and regressions
sections.summary: The anatomy of a reproducible bug report, logs and stack traces, refactoring versus rewriting, and regressions, with a failing test as the first step of a fix.

sections.title: Version control and tests
sections.summary: Repository, working tree, commit, branch, diff, merge, rebase and pull request in Git’s own terms (Pro Git); unit, integration and end-to-end tests as acceptance criteria an agent can run.

chapters.title: Coding Agents and Context Engineering
chapters.summary: How agentic coding tools work and how to set them up: the agent loop and permissions, context engineering, project instruction files, skills, subagents, hooks and the Model Context Protocol, all taught as dated vendor documentation over durable principles (least privilege, sandboxing, human approval, separation of untrusted input), and the security habits that keep an agent from being turned against you.
chapters.challenge: Set up Lamplighter for a coding agent: a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md under 60 lines, one skill, one hook that runs the tests after every edit, and a written permission policy. Use plan mode to add one feature, then write a short note on which file or setting changed the agent’s behavior and how you know.

sections.title: The agent loop: tools, permissions and plan mode
sections.summary: How an agent reads, runs and edits in a loop, permission modes and sandboxes, and the explore, plan, implement, commit workflow built around a check the agent can run.

sections.title: Context engineering and project instruction files
sections.summary: Curating what the agent sees: CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md (short, specific and advisory, per vendor docs as of October 2026), notes files, clearing and compaction, and the practitioner and vendor advice that a fresh session with a better prompt beats a long one full of corrections.

sections.title: Skills, subagents, hooks and MCP
sections.summary: On-demand skills, subagents with their own context, deterministic hooks and MCP servers for outside tools: what each is for and when to use which, as documented in October 2026.

sections.title: Prompt injection and safe agents
sections.summary: How instructions hidden in web pages, files and tool output can hijack an agent (prompt injection), why no prompt fully prevents it, and the established security principles that do help: least privilege, sandboxes, human approval, and never combining private data, untrusted content and a way to send data out.

chapters.title: Interface Vocabulary: UI, Interaction and Motion
chapters.summary: The names for what is on a screen and how it behaves, from the standards and references designers and developers share: CSS units and layout terms (MDN), type scale and hierarchy, components and their states, WCAG 2.2 success criteria by number, WAI-ARIA 1.2 roles, states and properties, design tokens, Nielsen Norman Group usability vocabulary, and motion in milliseconds and named easing curves.
chapters.challenge: Specify Lamplighter’s title screen, pause menu and settings screen in words alone: layout, components, every state, breakpoints, contrast and target-size criteria, and three microinteractions with timing. Have an AI build them, take screenshots, and compare the result with your spec item by item.

sections.title: Layout, spacing, type and hierarchy
sections.summary: Grids, columns, gutters, margins and padding, spacing scales in px and rem, type scale, weight and line height, and the visual hierarchy that tells the eye where to go first.

sections.title: Components and their states
sections.summary: Buttons, modals, toasts, drawers, tabs and menus, the states every component needs (default, hover, focus, active, disabled, loading, empty and error), and the WAI-ARIA 1.2 roles, states and properties that name them for assistive technology.

sections.title: Responsive design, accessibility and design tokens
sections.summary: Breakpoints, touch targets, and WCAG 2.2 success criteria cited by number (1.4.3 contrast, 2.4.7 focus visible, 2.5.8 target size), keyboard rules, and naming design decisions as tokens an AI can reuse.

sections.title: Feedback, flows and motion
sections.summary: Affordances and feedback, user flows and onboarding, microinteractions as trigger, rules, feedback and loops, and motion specs in milliseconds with CSS easing functions (ease-out, cubic-bezier), the animation principles of slow in and slow out, and reduced-motion alternatives.

chapters.title: Image Generation and Visual Art
chapters.summary: The language of pictures for image models, taught from photography’s and cinematography’s durable terms (shot size, camera angle, focal length in millimetres, aperture and depth of field, key, fill and rim light, color temperature in kelvin, hex colors) and then each tool’s documented controls, labeled as dated vendor guidance.
chapters.challenge: Write a visual style guide for Lamplighter (palette in hex, lighting, medium, framing, a reusable style block and one approved hero image) and use it to generate a title illustration, a character concept sheet and a background that look like one family. Record each prompt, tool and date in the prompt log.

sections.title: The anatomy of an image prompt
sections.summary: Subject, context and style as the core slots, then composition, light, palette, mood and format; sentences versus keyword piles; and describing what you want instead of what you don’t.

sections.title: Composition, camera and light
sections.summary: Rule of thirds, negative space, shot sizes and camera angles from film grammar (Bordwell, Thompson and Smith), focal length and depth of field, three-point lighting (key, fill and rim), time of day, color temperature and color-grading terms.

sections.title: Style, medium, references and consistency
sections.summary: Naming mediums and techniques precisely, describing a style instead of naming a living artist, style and character references, and a style block that keeps a set of images consistent.

sections.title: Tool controls, as documented
sections.summary: Aspect ratio, resolution, seeds, negative-prompt fields, inpainting, outpainting, upscaling, text in images and transparent backgrounds, with which tools support what as of October 2026.

chapters.title: Video, Camera Language and Animation
chapters.summary: Directing moving pictures with film grammar and animation’s classic vocabulary: shot sizes and camera moves (Bordwell, Thompson and Smith), standard frame rates (24, 25, 29.97/30 and 60 fps, as named in SMPTE timecode), the twelve principles of animation (Thomas and Johnston, 1981), game animation assets, and prompting video models with camera-first structure, image-to-video, keyframes and native audio, as documented by each vendor in October 2026.
chapters.challenge: Write a shot list and animation spec for Lamplighter’s 20-second intro cutscene and its player sprite (idle, run, jump, land), with camera moves, frame counts and loop points. Generate or brief each shot from approved stills and check every clip against the shot list.

sections.title: Shots, cuts and camera moves
sections.summary: Shot sizes in sequence, the 180-degree rule, pan, tilt, dolly, truck, pedestal, crane, orbit and handheld, zoom versus dolly, and cut types.

sections.title: Frame rate, timing and game animation assets
sections.summary: Frames per second and the standard rates, keyframes and in-betweens, animating on ones and twos, the twelve principles of animation as working vocabulary, and sprite sheets, frame counts, loops, pivots and animation states.

sections.title: Prompting video models
sections.summary: Vendor guidance, dated: camera first, then subject, action, setting and style; one action per clip; describing only motion in image-to-video; positive phrasing; and start and end frames for loops and transitions, with the reasoning that makes each habit likely to outlast the tool.

sections.title: Consistency, extension and sound in generated video
sections.summary: Keeping characters and looks stable across clips with references and approved stills, extending scenes, prompting native dialogue and sound, and when to make the audio separately.

chapters.title: Audio, Music and Voice
chapters.summary: The words of sound for games and apps, anchored in published standards: sample rate and bit depth, loudness in LUFS and true peak in dBTP as defined by ITU-R BS.1770 with EBU R 128’s broadcast target, the mixing terms engineers use, prompting music generators for loops and adaptive layers, sound effects from transient to tail, and directing synthetic voices with W3C SSML and each tool’s documented controls, dated.
chapters.challenge: Write Lamplighter’s audio brief: a music cue sheet with BPM, key, bars and loop points, an SFX list with layers and delivery format, loudness targets, and voice direction for two lines of dialogue with pronunciation notes. Generate at least one item of each kind and check it against the brief.

sections.title: Digital audio basics and loudness
sections.summary: Sample rate, bit depth and file formats, peak versus loudness, LUFS, true peak and headroom as defined in ITU-R BS.1770, EBU R 128’s −23 LUFS broadcast target, and platform and game targets given as dated vendor or industry guidance.

sections.title: Mixing vocabulary
sections.summary: EQ, compression, reverb and delay, panning, mono and stereo, stems and ducking, in the terms engineers use.

sections.title: Prompting music for games
sections.summary: Genre, instrumentation, BPM, key and meter in a style prompt, section tags, loops with no intro or ending, stingers, and vertical layering and horizontal resequencing.

sections.title: Sound effects and voice direction
sections.summary: Layering an SFX from transient to tail, foley and one action per file, dry and mono delivery, and directing a voice by intent, pace, pitch and emphasis with W3C SSML 1.1 elements (break, prosody, emphasis, phoneme, say-as), the IPA for pronunciation, and each tool’s audio tags as it documents them, dated.

chapters.title: Game Design Vocabulary
chapters.summary: The words designers use for how a game works and feels, from the field’s established frameworks and texts (MDA, Schell’s lenses, Swink’s game feel, Fullerton’s formal elements, flow): loops, mechanics, game feel, collision, difficulty, economy, progression and level design, with practitioner terms such as coyote time and juice labeled as such and given in exact units.
chapters.challenge: Write Lamplighter’s game design one-pager and a tuning table (jump height, coyote time, input buffer, i-frames) in exact units, have an AI implement it, and playtest two variants.

sections.title: Core loops, mechanics and goals
sections.summary: Core loop, mechanics, rules and goals, Fullerton’s formal elements (players, objectives, procedures, rules, resources, conflict, boundaries, outcome) and the MDA framework (Hunicke, LeBlanc and Zubek, 2004) as a shared language.

sections.title: Game feel and juice
sections.summary: Input, response, hitboxes and hurtboxes, coyote time, input buffering, i-frames, hit-stop, screen shake and particles: Swink’s game-feel vocabulary plus practitioner terms, each labeled and specified in frames, milliseconds or pixels.

sections.title: Difficulty, progression and economy
sections.summary: Difficulty curves, flow, sources and sinks, progression and unlocks.

sections.title: Level design words
sections.summary: Critical path, gating, landmarks, teaching through level design, pacing and set pieces.

chapters.title: Game Art and 3D: Sprites, Meshes, Materials and Budgets
chapters.summary: Vocabulary for game art in 2D and 3D, anchored in the glTF 2.0 standard (ISO/IEC 12113) and the Blender Manual: sprites, tilesets, pixel art and projections, meshes and UVs, the PBR metallic-roughness material model, rigging, shaders and performance budgets, and what image and 3D generators can and cannot deliver, as documented and dated.
chapters.challenge: Specify a 16-tile rooftop tileset and a low-poly 3D diorama of Lamplighter’s rooftop for the title screen: grid size, palette, projection, polycount, texel density, material list and a frame-time budget. Generate or brief both, check them against the spec, and fix what the generator got wrong.

sections.title: 2D game art: sprites, tilesets and pixel art
sections.summary: Sprites and sprite sheets, tilesets and autotiles, pixel-art resolution and palettes, isometric and orthographic projection, 9-slice UI and texture atlases.

sections.title: Meshes, topology and UVs
sections.summary: Vertices, edges and faces, quads and triangles, edge flow, normals, units and axes (glTF uses metres and +Y up), and UV unwrapping, in Blender Manual terms.

sections.title: PBR materials and textures
sections.summary: The glTF 2.0 metallic-roughness model (base color, metallic, roughness, normal, occlusion and emissive maps), tileable textures, texel density and texture resolution, and why generated images need flat albedo.

sections.title: Rigging, shaders and performance
sections.summary: Skeletons, skinning and weights, shaders, real-time and baked lighting, level of detail, draw calls and frame-time budgets.

chapters.title: Directing AI on a Whole Project
chapters.summary: Running a whole project with AI help: requirements documents in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148’s terms, small verified steps with a definition of done, evals for the prompts you rely on, review and handoffs between tools, and versioned prompts and project memory, with spec-driven development taught as a recent practitioner and vendor method, labeled as such.
chapters.challenge: Assemble the Lamplighter project binder (PRD, design doc, style guide, audio brief, prompt kit, eval set, prompt log and project instruction file) and use it to take one feature from spec to merged, reviewed, playable build, with eval results before and after each prompt change.

sections.title: PRDs, design docs and spec-driven development
sections.summary: Product requirements and requirements traceability in ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148’s terms, game design documents, art and audio bibles, and the specify, plan, tasks, implement sequence of spec-driven development (a recent practitioner and vendor method, dated).

sections.title: Planning in small, verified steps
sections.summary: Milestones, vertical slices, task lists and a definition of done (the Scrum Guide’s term) that an agent can work through, with a check at every step.

sections.title: Evals and LLM judges
sections.summary: Turning success criteria into a small test set, code-based, model-based and human grading, rubric judges and their position, length and self-preference biases, and rerunning evals whenever a model or prompt changes.

sections.title: Review, handoffs and versioned prompts
sections.summary: Review checklists, fresh-context reviewers, diffs and playtests, passing work between chat, coding, image and audio tools without losing the spec, and prompt logs and changelogs kept in Git and numbered with Semantic Versioning.

preface:
This book is for people who make things by asking. You describe a game, a screen, a picture or a sound to an AI, and it makes something. Often it makes something close, and then you spend an hour pushing it toward what you meant. The distance between what you pictured and what you got is mostly a distance in words. Designers, developers, animators, sound engineers and game designers have spent decades naming the parts of their work precisely, and much of their writing is public text of the kind models learn from. So when you say “a 200 ms ease-out on the modal” instead of “make it smoother,” you are using words with one agreed meaning that people and models both tend to read the same way.

The first three chapters are about asking well: how to write a request as a spec, how language models actually behave, and which prompting habits still work in 2026. The vendors themselves now advise against several popular tips, from capital-letter warnings to “think step by step,” for their current models, and I will show you what they and the research say instead. Chapters 4 and 5 cover code and the coding agents that write it, including how to set up their context and keep them safe. The middle chapters go craft by craft: interfaces, images, video, audio and voice, game design, and game art and 3D. The last chapter puts it all together into a way of running a whole project. Every section ends with a Prompt kit, templates you can paste into a real tool today.

You will meet three kinds of statement in this book, and the prose always tells you which one you are reading. Established facts are standards, definitions, documented specifications and peer-reviewed findings, such as WCAG’s 4.5:1 contrast rule or the loudness measure in ITU-R BS.1770; I state them plainly and cite them. Vendor guidance is what a company’s documentation says about its own tools; I name the company and the month (“Anthropic’s documentation, as of October 2026, advises...”) and give the reasoning that explains why it works, so the idea outlives the tool. Practice and opinion covers practitioner lore, expert judgment and popular techniques; I mark it (“many practitioners report...”, “the evidence is thin”) and say what is known about whether it holds. Take the second and third kinds with a grain of salt: they go out of date. When a tool fact matters to you, read the vendor’s current page and run your own small test before you rely on it.

Our running example is Lamplighter, a small 2D platformer for the web browser in which a lamplighter climbs rooftops at dusk, lighting lamps before night falls. You will specify it, build it with a coding agent, give it art, animation, music and sound, tune how it feels to play and, by Chapter 12, keep it all in a project binder that any AI can pick up and continue. Tools and model names change every few months, so when I name a specific feature I give the month I checked it. The principles underneath last much longer, and I always teach them first.

bible.teacher: Dr. Professor teaches this book as a working director of AI tools who also knows each craft’s own literature. Prompting advice comes from peer-reviewed research on language models and from Anthropic’s, OpenAI’s and Google’s current documentation, always attributed and dated; where vendors disagree, or the evidence is thin, the book says so. Each field’s durable vocabulary is the backbone, taught from its standards and specifications (ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148 for requirements, WCAG 2.2 and WAI-ARIA for accessibility, ITU-R BS.1770 and EBU R 128 for loudness, W3C SSML for synthetic voice, SMPTE timecode rates and film grammar for moving pictures, glTF 2.0 for 3D assets, Semantic Versioning and Git’s own terms for code) and from its standard texts (Schell and Swink for games, Tidwell and colleagues and WCAG for interfaces, Bordwell, Thompson and Smith for film, Senior for mixing) and from reference documentation such as MDN Web Docs, the Blender Manual and each generator’s own help pages. Every term is defined, shown in a before and after prompt, tied to something you can check in the result, and, where it helps, packaged as a copyable template.
bible.promise: By the last page you will be able to describe what you want from any AI tool in the precise terms of the craft involved, write it as a spec with checkable acceptance criteria, give an agent the right context and no more, judge the output against the spec with tests, reviews and small evals, and run a project from first prompt to finished game.
threads: A good request is a spec: goal, context, constraints, acceptance criteria, examples and output format, stated as what you want rather than what you don’t, in calm, plain words.
Craft vocabulary is compression: one exact term (ease-out, rim light, dolly-in, LUFS, coyote time) replaces a paragraph of adjectives and is understood by people and models alike.
Make “done” checkable, then check it: numbers, units, states, tests and small evals, changing one thing at a time and versioning prompts like code.
Context is a budget: give the model what the task needs (the right files, notes, examples and references) and no more, because accuracy falls as context fills.

Durable principles first, dated details second, and every claim labeled: established facts (standards, definitions, peer-reviewed findings) are stated plainly with a citation; vendor guidance is attributed, dated and explained; practice and opinion are marked as such, because tools change every few months and the vocabulary of each craft does not.

runningExamples.name: Lamplighter
runningExamples.use: A small 2D platformer for the web browser, written in JavaScript, in which a lamplighter climbs city rooftops at dusk lighting lamps before night falls. Each chapter adds a part: the first spec (Ch. 1), model and prompt experiments (Ch. 2 and 3), code and bug reports (Ch. 4), agent setup with a project instruction file, skill and hook (Ch. 5), menus and HUD (Ch. 6), art (Ch. 7), cutscene and animation (Ch. 8), music, sound and voice (Ch. 9), tuning and levels (Ch. 10), tileset and 3D title diorama (Ch. 11) and the project binder with its eval set (Ch. 12). A worked example, not a real product.

runningExamples.name: Before and after prompt pairs
runningExamples.use: Every section shows a realistic vague request, the rewritten request using the section’s terms, and what each change prevents. Results are described, never presented as quotations of a specific model’s output.

runningExamples.name: The prompt kit
runningExamples.use: Copyable templates at the end of sections (spec skeletons, bug reports, image, video, music, SFX and voice briefs, review and eval prompts), each built only from techniques the chapter teaches. The reader adapts them for Lamplighter and files them in the project binder.

runningExamples.name: The project binder
runningExamples.use: The folder of documents the reader builds across the book: spec, style guide, audio brief, tuning table, prompt kit, eval set, prompt log and project instruction file, assembled in Chapter 12.

conventions: Evidence convention, signaled in the prose itself (no special formatting). Every factual statement is one of three kinds. (a) Established: standards, definitions, documented specifications and peer-reviewed findings, stated plainly with a citation (“WCAG 2.2 success criterion 1.4.3 requires 4.5:1 [2]”).

(b) Vendor guidance: what a company’s documentation says about its own tools, always attributed and dated (“Anthropic’s documentation, as of October 2026, advises...”), followed by the reasoning that explains why it works, so the idea outlives the tool. Vendor claims about their own internal tests are reported as claims (“Anthropic reports that in its own tests...”), never as findings.

(c) Practice and opinion: practitioner lore, expert opinion and popular techniques, marked in the sentence (“many practitioners report...”, “in my experience...”, “this is a popular claim; the evidence is mixed/thin”) together with what is known about whether it holds. Peer-reviewed results on older models carry their model generation and year, and the text says which part (the direction or the number) to carry forward.
The six-part spec, the project binder and similar frameworks are this book’s teaching devices, and the text says so; they are not presented as industry standards.
Bold each key term at first use and define it in one sentence; reuse the same term afterwards (do not alternate synonyms).

Quote prompts in typographic quotes and label them Before and After; keep them short enough to type. Write example prompts in calm, plain language; capitals and “CRITICAL” appear only when the text is showing the anti-pattern.

Teach the durable principle first, then the tool-specific detail. Date every tool-specific fact (model names, parameters, defaults, limits, feature support) with “as of October 2026” or the month checked, and cite the vendor’s documentation page. Model names are examples, not recommendations.
Never invent a feature, parameter, limit or price. A claim found only in third-party guides is worded as such (“third-party guides report”); a claim nobody could confirm is left out.

Mark advice that has changed: when a once-standard technique (prefill, temperature 0, “think step by step”, ALL-CAPS emphasis) appears, say what it was for, what current vendor guidance says instead, and for which models.
Give measurable quantities with units: px and rem, ms, fps, Hz and kHz, bits, dB, LUFS and dBTP, BPM, tokens.

Use the field’s reference documentation for definitions: MDN Web Docs for web terms, Nielsen Norman Group articles for UX terms, WCAG 2.2 for accessibility, the Blender Manual for 3D terms, vendor docs for model and generator behavior.
Italicize game and film titles and give the release year at first mention.
Prompt kit templates use [BRACKETED PLACEHOLDERS], must work when pasted into a real tool today, and use only techniques the chapter teaches and its sources support.
Refer back to earlier chapters by number and to Lamplighter’s project binder by document name.

bible.care: AI tools, model names, features, limits and prices change every few months, and so does vendor advice. Tool facts expire: every vendor statement carries its month, and the reader is shown how to re-check it (open the vendor’s current documentation page and compare; then run a small eval of their own, the same prompt on three to five fixed inputs before and after any change of model, setting or wording, scored against written criteria). Teach the durable concept first; give any tool-specific detail with the month it was checked and its documentation page, word third-party-only claims as such, and never invent or guess a feature, parameter or setting of a specific tool. Mark outdated techniques plainly (for example, assistant prefill and non-default temperature return errors on the newest Claude models as of October 2026). Do not present imagined model outputs as real quotations. Treat generated code as unreviewed until tested. Never paste secrets (API keys, passwords) into prompts, project instruction files or public repositories. Agents act with your permissions: teach least privilege, sandboxes and human approval for destructive or outward-facing actions, warn that hooks and MCP servers run code on your machine, and state plainly that no prompt reliably stops prompt injection, so an agent with access to private data should not read untrusted content while it can also send data out. Respect copyright and likeness: prompt for styles by describing their techniques rather than naming living artists to copy, do not clone a real person’s voice or face without consent, and follow each tool’s terms and licenses for commercial use.
